extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers interested in Jorge Luis Borges's life, works, and literary techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for emulating or analyzing Jorge Luis Borges's short fiction and related literary practices: concision, thematic motifs (labyrinths, mirrors, libraries), non-linearity, translation approach, and use of pseudo‑epigrapha.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for the short story and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges preferred the short story as "an essential genre" and rejected the novel as requiring "padding"; he wrote that composing vast books is a "laborious and impoverishing folly" and that an idea that can be perfectly related orally in a few minutes need not be set out over hundreds of pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor brevity and concentrated effect: express core ideas succinctly, avoid unnecessary expansion or 'padding' that dilutes an idea. Example: his longest fiction is a fourteen‑page story; prologue to Ficciones argues against 500‑page expositions of a single idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing fact and fantasy (blending the real and the fantastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many stories mix realistic South American life (folk heroes, gauchos, detectives, historical figures) with fantastical themes (a library with every possible text, a man who forgets nothing, an artifact showing everything in the universe). Borges 'mixed the real and the fantastic, fact with fiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave verisimilitude and the fantastic so the reader accepts improbable conceits; use ordinary settings or historical references as anchors for speculative elements (examples: "The Library of Babel", "Funes, the Memorious", "The Aleph").

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring thematic preoccupations: time, infinity, mirrors, labyrinths
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges's best‑known stories repeatedly deal with themes of time ("The Secret Miracle"), infinity ("The Aleph"), mirrors ("Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius"), and labyrinths ("The Garden of Forking Paths", "The House of Asterion", etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these themes central or structural: use temporal puzzles, paradoxes of infinity, reflective doubling, and maze imagery as organizing principles for plot and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative non‑linearity and the forking paths motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges popularized the idea of forking paths: networks of time in which branches represent different choices and endings, none of which is unique — a model of non‑linear narrative where multiple equally valid outcomes coexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narratives that present branching possibilities, parallel timelines, or non‑sequential structure; treat multiple outcomes as philosophically meaningful rather than mere gimmicks (example: "The Garden of Forking Paths").

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific symbolic motifs (labyrinth, mirror, library, map, book, dream)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note recurring images in Borges's work — the Labyrinth, the Mirror, the Library, the Map, the Book, and the Dream — used to question or play with the nature of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ these motifs as metaphors and structural devices to explore epistemological questions; a story invoking a 'library' might be about totality and combinatorics, a 'mirror' about identity and reflection, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of mythology, mathematics, and theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Paramount among Borges's intellectual interests were mythology, mathematics, and theology, which he integrated through literature 'sometimes playfully, sometimes with great seriousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on cross‑disciplinary material (mythic tropes, mathematical concepts, theological puzzles) to enrich speculative premises and to frame philosophical problems within fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating 'poetic faith' and managing suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Williamson summarizes Borges's contention that 'fiction did not depend on the illusion of reality; what mattered ultimately was an author's ability to generate "poetic faith" in his reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize cultivating a readerly acceptance of the story's conventions ('poetic faith') rather than strict mimetic realism; the ethical is to create internal consistency and evocative authority that persuades the reader to engage with the fiction's premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation philosophy: translations may improve or be unfaithful; multiple renderings valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges lectured that a translation may improve upon the original, may even be unfaithful to it, and that alternative and potentially contradictory renderings of the same work can be equally valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating (or reworking source texts), allow for adaptive, interpretive choices; fidelity to surface detail is not the sole criterion — capture the work's effects and be open to multiple legitimate renderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudo‑epigrapha and literary forgery
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges employed devices of literary forgery and the review of imaginary works (pseudo‑epigrapha): summaries, commentaries, and notes on non‑existent books (inspired by works such as Carlyle's Sartor Resartus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent fictional texts, reviews, or scholarly apparatus as a narrative device: present fake bibliographies, fragmentary commentaries, or 'notes' that expand the world and play with authorial authority (examples: A Universal History of Infamy, notes on imaginary books).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erudition and the aesthetic of 'out‑of‑the‑way' learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges often indulged in 'useless and out‑of‑the‑way erudition' — learned references and obscure scholarship deployed for their own intellectual pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective, sometimes obscure scholarship and literary allusion to create texture and intellectual resonance; avoid showing off gratuitously, but allow erudition to illuminate thematic concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse sexual content and marginalization of women in narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex and women are largely absent from Borges's fiction; when present, women often occupy secondary roles or function as objects rather than subjects. Sexual scenes are rare and typically elliptically narrated (exception: 'Emma Zunz').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If emulating Borges, portray gender and sexuality with restraint and often as peripheral to the central intellectual or metaphysical concerns; be mindful that this is a characteristic of Borges's oeuvre, not a normative model for inclusive representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as philosophical riddle: using stories to pose ontological questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges's narratives often operate as philosophical puzzles (e.g., questions of whether the writer writes the story or vice versa — the 'Borgesian conundrum'), using literary form to probe ontology and authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame plots as thought experiments: let narrative conceits instantiate metaphysical or epistemological puzzles rather than merely drive plot; invite readers into interpretive uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and creation of 'precursors' (work that reshapes readings of earlier texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges argued that every writer 'creates his own precursors' — later work modifies how earlier texts are read; his heavy intertextuality deliberately reorders literary history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave explicit and implicit references to other works so the new text reframes or refracts antecedent writings; treat influence as active reconfiguration rather than passive reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes and ambivalent moral portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Borges sometimes constructs archetypes to explore tragic or ambivalent moral situations (e.g., inventing an 'ideal Nazi' in 'Deutsches Requiem' to examine the tragic fate of an extremist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archetypal figures to dramatize ethical ambiguity; present characters who embody extreme ideas to allow literary and philosophical exploration rather than straightforward moralizing.
